reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Caused by defective mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal enzymes, so multiple enzymes are mislocalised rather than a single enzyme being deficient
Clinically resembles a severe mucopolysaccharidosis with early onset of coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, and organomegaly, but usually without corneal clouding or urinary glycosaminoglycan excess
Characteristic phase-dense cytoplasmic inclusions in cultured fibroblasts give the disease its name
Presents in early infancy with growth failure, gingival hypertrophy, and skeletal changes, often noted at or soon after birth
A key diagnostic clue is markedly elevated activity of several lysosomal enzymes in plasma or serum, with correspondingly low intracellular activity
Caused by variants in GNPTAB affecting the alpha/beta subunits of GlcNAc-1-phosphotransferase
Mucolipidosis III (pseudo-Hurler polydystrophy) is the milder, allelic or related disorder in the same pathway
reference.pathophysiology: I-cell disease results from deficiency of the enzyme UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, encoded (alpha/beta subunits) by GNPTAB. This enzyme adds the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker that normally directs newly synthesised lysosomal hydrolases to the lysosome. Without the marker, multiple enzymes are instead secreted into the extracellular space, so lysosomes are depleted of hydrolases and undigested substrates accumulate as characteristic inclusion bodies within cells. The biochemical signature is therefore paradoxical: low intracellular lysosomal enzyme activity but high activity of the same enzymes in plasma. Widespread lysosomal dysfunction produces severe multisystem storage disease. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Hurler syndrome and other severe mucopolysaccharidoses
Sly syndrome (MPS VII) presenting in infancy
Congenital hypothyroidism given the coarse features
Other storage disorders with early coarse facies and skeletal dysplasia
additionalInvestigations: Plasma or serum assay of multiple lysosomal enzymes, showing markedly raised activity
Cultured fibroblast studies demonstrating low intracellular enzyme activity and inclusion bodies
Urinary glycosaminoglycan analysis, typically not markedly elevated, helping distinguish it from mucopolysaccharidoses
Echocardiography and developmental assessment for systemic involvement
redFlags: Severe early growth failure and feeding difficulty
Progressive cardiorespiratory compromise from valvular and airway involvement
reference.prognosis: The disorder is severe and progressive, with cardiorespiratory complications commonly limiting survival to early childhood. Management is supportive, as no established disease-modifying therapy exists.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as a mucopolysaccharidosis and being misled by near-normal urinary glycosaminoglycans
Overlooking the diagnostic value of raised plasma lysosomal enzyme activity
Attributing coarse facies at birth to congenital hypothyroidism alone
Failing to distinguish severe ML II from the milder ML III phenotype
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
